# Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta (MN 136 (PTS MN iii 207))

**ID:** MN 136 (PTS MN iii 207)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Longer Analysis of Deeds
**PTS:** MN iii 207

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahākammavibhaṅga Sutta* (MN 136, PTS MN iii 207) is set at the Squirrels' Feeding Place in the Bamboo Grove near Rājagaha, opening after an encounter between the venerable Samiddhi and the wanderer Potaliputta [Jetjiravat]. Confronted with simplistic and dogmatic assertions regarding the mechanics of action, the Buddha provides a detailed analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of intentional deeds and their consequences [SuttaCentral; Flores 2008; Martini]. Rejecting premature generalizations derived from limited supernormal vision by outside contemplatives, the Buddha sets out the nuances of the ten wholesome and unwholesome courses of action [Flores 2008; Martini]. He demonstrates that karmic fruition is not rigidly immediate or monolithic: an individual habitual to evil deeds may nevertheless take rebirth in a heavenly realm, or a virtuous person in a state of deprivation, due to other past actions or the specific state of mind and views held at the moment of death [Sieg 2004; Langer 2007; Gethin; Ñāṇamoli & Bodhi 1995; Anālayo 2016].

Curated parallels recorded for the sutta include MĀ 171 in the Chinese *Madhyama-āgama*, Up 5.003 in Śamathadeva's Tibetan *Abhidharmakośopāyikā-ṭīkā*, and citations in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa* (T 1509) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus strongly aligns the text with both MĀ (ZH_T01_0026) and the Tibetan *Upāyikā* (D4094), in agreement with SuttaCentral, while also identifying cross-language reuse in Sanskrit works such as the *Divyāvadāna* and *Yogācārabhūmi* [DharmaNexus]. In Pali literature, the discourse shares extensive doctrinal material with the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (notably AN 10, AN 3, and AN 4), the *Brahmajāla Sutta* (DN 1), the *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), and its companion text, the *Cūḷakammavibhaṅga Sutta* (MN 135) [DharmaNexus]. It is additionally cited in canonical and paracanonical treatises including the *Nettippakaraṇa* (Ne 9) and *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 8.9), as well as discussed extensively across Pali commentaries and the *Visuddhimagga-mahāṭīkā* [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Langer 2007].
